newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices to get boost from latest Iraqi fighting.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices to get boost from latest Iraqi fighting.

text.p: Oil prices look set to rally on Monday as new tensions in Iraq are seen threatening supplies from the Middle East.
Iraqi military intervention in inter-Kurd fighting over the town of Arbil in northern Iraq has occurred at a time when global oil inventories are low and world oil demand is booming.

Traders say world benchmark North Sea Brent Blend crude oil should top $21 a barrel and hit their highest levels in more than four months in nervous reaction to Iraqi warnings to the United States on Sunday to keep out.
Oil prices are already running some $4 above year-ago levels and analysts said they saw no sign of any immediate retreat.

"There is no reason why Brent should not hit above $21 tomorrow. With all the tensions in the Middle East right now and in a balanced market, oil prices should stay firm for some time to come," said Geoff Pyne, oil economist at Swiss Bank UBS.
Pyne said the latest conflict may put off indefinitely the return of Iraqi oil exports.
October Brent closed up four cents at $20.78 on Friday amid renewed speculation that the May 21 oil-for-food deal with the United Nations might get further delayed.
"The question now may be not when will Iraqi oil sales start but whether they will start," Pyne said.

President Bill Clinton put U.S. troops in the Gulf on high alert after Saturday's attack on Arbil. Iraq warned Washington to stay out of its Kurdish north and vowed to turn it into another Vietnam if Washington intervened.
In recent months, oil prices have been supported by heightened tensions between the U.S., the world's largest oil consumer, and several major Mideast oil producers.

In its campaign against guerrilla violence, Washington implemented a law targeting foreign companies doing business with Iran and Libya, two members of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries.

The U.S. is still investigating the truck bomb that killed 19 Americans at al-Khobar military complex in Saudi Arabia on June 25 as well as the mystery crash of TWA Flight 800 off the coast of New York. Both incidents drove oil prices higher given their possible links with Middle East guerrillas.
"There have already been worries in the market about the Middle East so the Iraqi incident will make traders that much more cautious about selling oil given the uncertainties," UBS's Pyne said.
The delay in implementing the Iraqi oil sale plan has led nervous traders to cover oversold positions they had built in expectation of the additional supplies of about 700,000 barrels per day (bpd).

"We are strong now because the Iraqi oil is not there yet. Even when it does come back it will not be before the first couple of cargoes hit the market before we see the price impact," said Bo Van Wijk, vice president of energy risk management services at Swiss bank UBS.
Low stocks of heating oil and diesel (distillates), rising demand from major industrialised nations and delays in the startup of new oil fields in the North Sea have added to the oil rally.
"The demand picture in the third quarter looks much stronger than previously expected, especially in the OECD countries," Washington oil consultancy Petroleum Finance Co said in a recent report.
